claim: Abl2 regulates myofiber length in the diaphragm muscle.
source: We show that Abelson tyrosine-protein kinase 2 (Abl2) has a key role in regulating myofiber length, as a loss of Abl2 leads to excessively long myofibers in the diaphragm, intercostal and levator auris muscles but not limb muscles.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that Abl2−/− mice have longer myofibers in the diaphragm muscle compared to wild type mice, supported by measurements and images.

claim: Loss of Abl2 leads to excessively long myofibers in intercostal muscles.
source: We show that Abelson tyrosine-protein kinase 2 (Abl2) has a key role in regulating myofiber length, as a loss of Abl2 leads to excessively long myofibers in the diaphragm, intercostal and levator auris muscles but not limb muscles.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that muscle fibers in intercostal muscles extend over multiple ribs in Abl2 mutant mice.

claim: Loss of Abl2 leads to excessively long myofibers in levator auris muscles.
source: We show that Abelson tyrosine-protein kinase 2 (Abl2) has a key role in regulating myofiber length, as a loss of Abl2 leads to excessively long myofibers in the diaphragm, intercostal and levator auris muscles but not limb muscles.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that muscle fibers in the levator auris longus muscle appear wavy in Abl2 mutant mice.

claim: Loss of Abl2 does not affect myofiber length in limb muscles.
source: We show that Abelson tyrosine-protein kinase 2 (Abl2) has a key role in regulating myofiber length, as a loss of Abl2 leads to excessively long myofibers in the diaphragm, intercostal and levator auris muscles but not limb muscles.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing no evidence for an increase in muscle fiber length in hindlimb muscles.

claim: Increased myofiber length in Abl2 mutants is caused by enhanced myoblast proliferation.
source: Increased myofiber length is caused by enhanced myoblast proliferation, expanding the pool of myoblasts and leading to increased myoblast fusion.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased EdU incorporation in Abl2 mutant myoblasts both in vivo and in vitro.

claim: Enhanced myoblast proliferation in Abl2 mutants leads to increased myoblast fusion.
source: Increased myofiber length is caused by enhanced myoblast proliferation, expanding the pool of myoblasts and leading to increased myoblast fusion.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that the increase in muscle fiber length is accompanied by a proportional increase in myonuclei number.

claim: Abl2 acts in myoblasts to regulate muscle fiber length.
source: Abl2 acts in myoblasts, but as a consequence of expansion of the diaphragm muscle, the diaphragm central tendon is reduced in size, likely contributing to reduced stamina of Abl2 mutant mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from conditional knockout experiments showing that inactivation of Abl2 in myoblasts, but not in myofibers, leads to the muscle phenotype.

claim: Loss of Abl2 in myoblasts leads to reduction in size of the diaphragm central tendon.
source: Abl2 acts in myoblasts, but as a consequence of expansion of the diaphragm muscle, the diaphragm central tendon is reduced in size, likely contributing to reduced stamina of Abl2 mutant mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that the area of the central tendon, circumscribed by Scx expression, was reduced in Abl2−/− mice.

claim: Reduction in central tendon size likely contributes to reduced stamina of Abl2 mutant mice.
source: Abl2 acts in myoblasts, but as a consequence of expansion of the diaphragm muscle, the diaphragm central tendon is reduced in size, likely contributing to reduced stamina of Abl2 mutant mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that Abl2 mutant mice run less than wild type littermates, and this is attributed to replacement of the central tendon with muscle.

claim: Ectopic muscle islands form within the central tendon of Abl2+/− mice.
source: Ectopic muscle islands, each composed of myofibers of uniform length and orientation, form within the central tendon of Abl2+/− mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents images showing ectopic muscle islands in the central tendon of Abl2+/− mice.

claim: Myofibers within ectopic muscle islands in Abl2+/− mice are uniform in length.
source: Ectopic muscle islands, each composed of myofibers of uniform length and orientation, form within the central tendon of Abl2+/− mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents images showing that individual muscle fibers within an island were uniform in length.

claim: Myofibers within ectopic muscle islands in Abl2+/− mice are uniform in orientation.
source: Ectopic muscle islands, each composed of myofibers of uniform length and orientation, form within the central tendon of Abl2+/− mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents images showing that individual muscle fibers within an island were aligned with respect to one another.

claim: Specialized tendon cells form at the ends of ectopic muscle islands in Abl2+/− mice.
source: Specialized tendon cells, resembling tendon cells at myotendinous junctions, form at the ends of these muscle islands, suggesting that myofibers induce differentiation of tendon cells, which reciprocally regulate myofiber length and orientation.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that Scx RNA expression was enhanced in tendon cells that are juxtaposed to the ends of the ectopic muscle islands.

claim: Myofibers induce differentiation of tendon cells.
source: Specialized tendon cells, resembling tendon cells at myotendinous junctions, form at the ends of these muscle islands, suggesting that myofibers induce differentiation of tendon cells, which reciprocally regulate myofiber length and orientation.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that Scx expression is enhanced at the ends of ectopic muscle islands, suggesting induction by muscle fibers.

claim: Tendon cells reciprocally regulate myofiber length and orientation.
source: Specialized tendon cells, resembling tendon cells at myotendinous junctions, form at the ends of these muscle islands, suggesting that myofibers induce differentiation of tendon cells, which reciprocally regulate myofiber length and orientation.
evidence: The manuscript suggests this based on the observation that myofibers within ectopic islands are uniform in length and orientation, and specialized tendon cells form at their ends.

claim: Muscle fibers in the diaphragm muscle are 1.7-fold longer in Abl2−/− mice than wild type littermate controls.
source: We measured the length of myofibers in the costal diaphragm muscle from insertion points at the ventral rib to the central tendon and found that muscle fibers in the diaphragm muscle are 1.7-fold longer in Abl2−/− mice than wild type littermate controls (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expansion of muscle in Abl2 mutants is first evident at E13.5 during development of the diaphragm muscle.
source: This expansion of muscle, is first evident at E13.5 during development of the diaphragm muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing differences at E13.5.

claim: Scleraxis (Scx) is highly expressed in tendon cells at the myotendinous junction.
source: We found that Scx, a transcription factor that is expressed in tendon precursor cells (Schweitzer et al., 2001), is highly expressed in tendon cells at the myotendinous junction (MTJ) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C and cites previous work on Scx expression.

claim: Intercostal muscle fibers in Abl2 mutant mice extend over multiple ribs.
source: We found that muscle fibers in intercostal muscles, which ordinarily extend from one rib to the adjacent rib, were likewise excessively long and extended over multiple ribs (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 2A showing intercostal muscle fibers extending over multiple ribs.

claim: Muscle fibers in the levator auris longus muscle appear wavy in Abl2 mutant mice.
source: Similarly, muscle fibers in the levator auris longus muscle, which normally terminate at a midline tendon boundary, appeared wavy (Figure 2B), suggesting that some of the increased length was accommodated by bending of the myofiber (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 2B showing wavy muscle fibers.

claim: The midline tendon domain in the levator auris longus muscle is smaller in Abl2−/− mice than control mice.
source: We found that the midline tendon domain, marked by GFP expression, was smaller in Abl2−/− than control mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 2B showing reduced midline tendon marked by Scx::GFP.

claim: Muscle fiber overgrowth and reduction in size of the midline tendon appear to be coordinated in the levator auris longus muscle.
source: Thus, muscle fiber overgrowth and a reduction in size of the midline tendon appear to be coordinated in the levator auris longus muscle, similar to the diaphragm muscle.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing both muscle lengthening and tendon reduction in the levator auris longus muscle.

claim: The muscle and tendon aberrations persist in adult Abl2 mutant mice.
source: Figure 2C shows that the muscle remained lengthened and the central tendon remained smaller in adult Abl2 mutant mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 2C showing persistent phenotype in adult mice.

claim: Myofiber cross-sectional area remains normal in Abl2 mutant mice throughout development and in adults.
source: Throughout development and in adults, myofibers are lengthened, while myofiber cross-sectional area remains normal (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data in Figure 2D showing normal cross-sectional area.

claim: The increase in muscle fiber length in Abl2 mutants is accompanied by a proportional increase in myonuclei number.
source: By both methods, we found that the increase in muscle fiber length was accompanied by a proportional increase in myonuclei number.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from two methods of counting myonuclei, both showing proportional increase.

claim: Abl2 is highly expressed in the diaphragm muscle and absent from the central tendon in E18.5 mice.
source: We found that Abl2 is highly expressed in the diaphragm muscle and absent from the central tendon in E18.5 mice (Figure 4A,B), suggesting that Abl2 acts in myoblasts and/or myofibers to regulate muscle growth.
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Abl2 expression is high in myoblasts and declines during differentiation.
source: We found that Abl2 expression is high in myoblasts and declines during differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data from C2C12 cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myoblasts, rather than myotubes, are the major source of Abl2 expression in muscle.
source: These results indicate that myoblasts, rather than myotubes, are the major source of Abl2 expression in muscle.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing Abl2 expression declines during differentiation from myoblasts to myotubes.

claim: Selective inactivation of Abl2 in pre-migratory myogenic precursor cells leads to muscle defects like those found in Abl2−/− mice.
source: Selective inactivation of Abl2 in pre-migratory myogenic precursor cells (Abl2f/−; Pax3cre) led to muscle defects like those found in Abl2−/− mice (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 4C,D showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Inactivation of Abl2 in committed myoblasts causes aberrations in muscle development identical to those found in Abl2−/− mice.
source: Likewise, inactivation of Abl2 in committed myoblasts (Abl2f/−; Myodicre) caused aberrations in muscle development identical to those found in Abl2−/− mice (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 4C,E showing identical phenotypes.

claim: Inactivation of Abl2 in myofibers does not cause a muscle phenotype.
source: In contrast, inactivation of Abl2 in myofibers (Abl2f/−; Mck::Cre) did not cause a muscle phenotype (Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 4F showing normal muscle development.

claim: Abl2 is required in myoblasts rather than multinucleated myotubes to regulate muscle and tendon growth.
source: These findings indicate that Abl2 is required in myoblasts rather than multinucleated myotubes to regulate muscle and tendon growth.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from conditional knockout experiments showing phenotype only when Abl2 is inactivated in myoblasts.

claim: Abl2 mutant mice run less than wild type littermates.
source: We found that Abl2 mutant mice ran less than wild type littermates (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents running wheel data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Limb muscle development is normal in Abl2 mutant mice.
source: Because limb muscle development and limb strength were normal in Abl2 mutant mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 5B), the decrease in running distance suggests that replacement of the central tendon with muscle in the diaphragm impaired respiration when challenged in an endurance task.
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing normal limb muscle length and cross-sectional area.

claim: Limb strength is normal in Abl2 mutant mice.
source: Because limb muscle development and limb strength were normal in Abl2 mutant mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 5B), the decrease in running distance suggests that replacement of the central tendon with muscle in the diaphragm impaired respiration when challenged in an endurance task.
evidence: The manuscript presents grip strength data in Figure 5B showing normal limb strength.

claim: Replacement of the central tendon with muscle in the diaphragm impairs respiration when challenged in an endurance task.
source: Because limb muscle development and limb strength were normal in Abl2 mutant mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 5B), the decrease in running distance suggests that replacement of the central tendon with muscle in the diaphragm impaired respiration when challenged in an endurance task.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that Abl2 mutant mice run less despite normal limb muscle and strength.

claim: Abl2 muscle-conditional mutant mice display reduced stamina on the running wheel.
source: Like Abl2 mutant mice, the Abl2 muscle-conditional mutant mice displayed reduced stamina on the running wheel (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents running wheel data in Figure 5A showing reduced running distance in muscle-conditional mutants.

claim: Replacement of tendon with muscle in the diaphragm impairs respiration leading to impaired physical endurance.
source: Together, these results suggest that replacement of tendon with muscle in the diaphragm impairs respiration leading to impaired physical endurance.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that muscle-conditional Abl2 mutant mice show reduced running performance.

claim: The number of slow myofibers is normal in Abl2f/−; Myodicre adult diaphragm muscle.
source: We therefore analyzed additional features of muscle differentiation in Abl2f/−; Myodicre adult diaphragm muscle and found that the number of slow myofibers was normal (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data in Figure 5C showing normal percentage of slow-twitch fibers.

claim: The decreased stamina of muscle conditional Abl2 mutant mice cannot be attributed to a failure to develop slow muscle fibers.
source: Therefore, the decreased stamina of muscle conditional Abl2 mutant mice cannot be attributed to a failure to develop slow muscle fibers.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing normal number of slow myofibers in Abl2 mutant mice.

claim: Muscle fibers in Abl2−/− adult mice display ultrastructural features characteristic of skeletal muscle.
source: Further, muscle fibers in Abl2−/− adult mice displayed ultrastructural features characteristic of skeletal muscle, as the organization of sarcomeres and muscle-tendon attachment sites appeared normal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents electron microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decreased physical performance of Abl2 mutant mice is not caused by a failure to build the contractile apparatus.
source: Thus, the decreased physical performance of Abl2 mutant mice is not caused by a failure to build the contractile apparatus and is more likely caused by the replacement of the elastic central tendon with less-tensile skeletal muscle.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing normal sarcomere organization and infers that the decreased performance is due to tendon replacement.

claim: The decreased physical performance of Abl2 mutant mice is more likely caused by the replacement of the elastic central tendon with less-tensile skeletal muscle.
source: Thus, the decreased physical performance of Abl2 mutant mice is not caused by a failure to build the contractile apparatus and is more likely caused by the replacement of the elastic central tendon with less-tensile skeletal muscle.
evidence: The manuscript infers this based on normal muscle ultrastructure and the observed replacement of tendon with muscle.

claim: At E14, the percentage of myoblasts that incorporated EdU is greater in Abl2 mutant mice than wild type mice.
source: At E14, the percentage of myoblasts that incorporated EdU was greater in Abl2 mutant mice than wild type mice (Figure 6A,B), indicating that a loss of Abl2 leads to increased proliferation of myoblasts in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents EdU incorporation data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: A loss of Abl2 leads to increased proliferation of myoblasts in vivo.
source: At E14, the percentage of myoblasts that incorporated EdU was greater in Abl2 mutant mice than wild type mice (Figure 6A,B), indicating that a loss of Abl2 leads to increased proliferation of myoblasts in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents EdU incorporation data showing increased proliferation in Abl2 mutant myoblasts.

claim: A similar number of MyoD+ myoblasts are isolated from wild type and Abl2 mutant mice at E18.5.
source: A similar number of MyoD+ myoblasts were isolated from wild type and Abl2 mutant mice at E18.5 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data in Figure 6D showing similar numbers of MyoD+ cells at initial plating.

claim: A higher percentage of Abl2 mutant myoblasts incorporate EdU than wild type control myoblasts in primary culture.
source: We found that a higher percentage of Abl2 mutant myoblasts incorporated EdU than wild type control myoblasts (69.7 ± 4.1% and 44.1 ± 2.6% mean±SEM respectively) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript presents EdU incorporation data in Figure 6E with quantitative values.

claim: Cells that do not express MyoD do not differ in EdU incorporation between Abl2 mutant and wild type cultures.
source: In contrast, cells that did not express MyoD, such as fibroblasts or tendon cells, did not differ in EdU incorporation (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript presents EdU incorporation data in Figure 6F showing no difference in MyoD− cells.

claim: Abl2 negatively regulates proliferation and expands the pool of myoblasts but not of other cell types in muscle tissue.
source: Thus, Abl2 negatively regulates proliferation and expands the pool of myoblasts but not of other cell types in muscle tissue.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased proliferation specifically in MyoD+ cells but not MyoD− cells.

claim: Abl2+/− myoblasts proliferate at a rate that is intermediate between wild type and Abl2 homozygous mutant myoblasts.
source: Further, we compared EdU incorporation among wild type, Abl2+/− and Abl2 mutant cells and found that Abl2+/− myoblasts proliferated at a rate that was intermediate between wild type and Abl2 homozygous mutant myoblasts (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript presents EdU incorporation data in Figure 6G showing intermediate proliferation rate.

claim: An increased number of mitotic myoblasts are found in Abl2−/− cultures compared to wild type littermate cultures.
source: We also examined proliferation of myoblasts by double-staining with antibodies to MyoD and phospho-histone H3, a marker specific for cells undergoing mitosis, which revealed an increased number of mitotic myoblasts in Abl2−/− cultures compared to wild type littermate cultures (Figure 6H,I).
evidence: The manuscript presents phospho-histone H3 staining data in Figure 6H,I.

claim: The longer myofibers in Abl2−/− mice arise from enhanced proliferation of Abl2−/− myoblasts.
source: These data indicate that the longer myofibers in Abl2−/− mice arise from enhanced proliferation of Abl2−/− myoblasts.
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple lines of evidence showing increased myoblast proliferation in Abl2 mutants.

claim: Under proliferative conditions, myotube formation is greater in cultures from Abl2−/− than wild type mice.
source: Under these conditions, myotube formation was greater in cultures from Abl2−/− than wild type mice, leading to a greater fusion index calculated by the ratio of fused myoblasts to total myoblasts (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The manuscript presents fusion index data in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Abl2 mutant myotubes contain more nuclei than wild type myotubes under proliferative conditions.
source: Consistent with these data, Abl2 mutant myotubes contained more nuclei than wild type myotubes (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data in Figure 7C showing more nuclei per myotube.

claim: Under non-proliferative conditions, wild type and Abl2−/− cultures have similar fusion indices.
source: Under these conditions, which are non-permissive for proliferation, wild type and Abl2−/− cultures had similar fusion indices (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The manuscript presents fusion index data in Figure 7D,E showing no difference under non-proliferative conditions.

claim: The longer myofibers in Abl2−/− mice arise from enhanced proliferation of Abl2−/− myoblasts, increasing the size of the available myoblast pool, rather than an enhanced propensity of myoblasts to fuse.
source: Together, these data indicate that the longer myofibers in Abl2−/− mice arise from enhanced proliferation of Abl2−/− myoblasts, increasing the size of the available myoblast pool, rather than an enhanced propensity of myoblasts to fuse.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased fusion only under proliferative conditions, not under non-proliferative conditions.

claim: The increase in myoblast proliferation is accommodated and balanced by rapid myoblast fusion, so that the myotubes in Abl2 mutant mice accrue more nuclei and elongate.
source: Because a similar number of MyoD+ myoblasts are isolated from wild type and Abl2 mutant mice at E18.5 (Figure 6D), our data suggest that the increase in myoblast proliferation is accommodated and balanced by rapid myoblast fusion, so that the myotubes in Abl2 mutant mice accrue more nuclei and elongate.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that similar numbers of myoblasts are isolated despite increased proliferation.

claim: Pax7-positive satellite cells are evenly distributed along the length of the diaphragm muscle fibers in Abl2 mutant and control mice.
source: We counted Pax7-positive muscle satellite cells in serial cross-sections of Abl2 mutant and control mice and found that Pax7-positive satellite cells were evenly distributed along the length of the diaphragm muscle fibers, and that total satellite cell number increased in Abl2−/− mice in proportion to the increase in muscle length (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents Pax7 staining data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Total satellite cell number increases in Abl2−/− mice in proportion to the increase in muscle length.
source: We counted Pax7-positive muscle satellite cells in serial cross-sections of Abl2 mutant and control mice and found that Pax7-positive satellite cells were evenly distributed along the length of the diaphragm muscle fibers, and that total satellite cell number increased in Abl2−/− mice in proportion to the increase in muscle length (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing proportional increase.

claim: Increased muscle length did not occur at the expense of establishing the satellite cell pool.
source: These findings indicate that increased muscle length did not occur at the expense of establishing the satellite cell pool and that Pax7-positive satellite cell numbers are established in proportion to muscle size.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing proportional increase in satellite cells with muscle length.

claim: Pax7-positive satellite cell numbers are established in proportion to muscle size.
source: These findings indicate that increased muscle length did not occur at the expense of establishing the satellite cell pool and that Pax7-positive satellite cell numbers are established in proportion to muscle size.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing proportional increase in satellite cells with muscle length.

claim: The number of ectopic muscle islands in Abl2+/− mice is variable.
source: The number of ectopic muscle islands as well as the number of muscle fibers within each island were variable (Figure 8B), but individual muscle fibers within an island were uniform in length and aligned with respect to one another.
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 8B showing variable numbers of islands.

claim: The number of muscle fibers within each ectopic island in Abl2+/− mice is variable.
source: The number of ectopic muscle islands as well as the number of muscle fibers within each island were variable (Figure 8B), but individual muscle fibers within an island were uniform in length and aligned with respect to one another.
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 8B showing variable numbers of fibers within islands.

claim: Muscle fibers within an ectopic island coordinate their orientation and length in a manner that is independent of contact with a preexisting specialized tendon cell border.
source: These findings suggest that the muscle fibers within an island coordinate their orientation and length, in a manner that is independent of contact with a preexisting specialized tendon cell border (Volk and VijayRaghavan, 1994).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that muscle fibers within ectopic islands are uniform in length and orientation despite being surrounded by non-specialized tendon.

claim: The orientation of ectopic islands is biased to align with the nearby diaphragm muscle.
source: Although the location of the ectopic islands within the central tendon was variable, the orientation of the ectopic islands was biased to align with the nearby diaphragm muscle (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing alignment with nearby muscle.

claim: Myoblasts aligned with developing myotubes in the diaphragm muscle may retain this orientation as they aberrantly migrate, proliferate and differentiate in the central tendon.
source: This alignment of the ectopic muscle islands with the nearby diaphragm muscle raises the possibility that myoblasts, which are aligned with developing myotubes in the diaphragm muscle, retain this orientation as they aberrantly migrate, proliferate and differentiate in the central tendon.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on this possibility based on the observed alignment of ectopic islands.

claim: Scx RNA expression is enhanced in tendon cells that are juxtaposed to the ends of the ectopic muscle islands.
source: We found that Scx RNA expression was enhanced in tendon cells that are juxtaposed to the ends of the ectopic muscle islands (Figure 8C).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data in Figure 8C showing enhanced Scx expression.

claim: Muscle fibers, even when displaced, provide signals to tendon cells, contributing to specialized features of tendon cells at MTJs.
source: These findings suggest that muscle fibers, even when displaced, provide signals to tendon cells, contributing to specialized features of tendon cells at MTJs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that Scx expression is enhanced at the ends of ectopic muscle islands.

claim: Scx-expressing cells contribute to tendon cells surrounding and intercalated between muscle fibers but do not contribute to the muscle fibers within the ectopic muscle islands.
source: We found that Scx-expressing cells contributed to tendon cells surrounding and intercalated between muscle fibers but did not contribute to the muscle fibers within the ectopic muscle islands (Figure 8D).
evidence: The manuscript presents lineage tracing data in Figure 8D.

claim: Tendon cell precursors do not switch their fate and convert to muscle to form the ectopic muscle islands in Abl2+/− mice.
source: These findings are inconsistent with the idea tendon cell precursors switched their fate and converted to muscle to form the ectopic muscle islands in Abl2+/− mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents lineage tracing data showing Scx-expressing cells do not contribute to muscle fibers in ectopic islands.

claim: Ectopic muscle islands form in Abl2f/+; Pax3cre mice.
source: Figure 8E shows that ectopic muscle islands form in Abl2f/+; Pax3cre mice, indicating that a loss of Abl2 in myogenic cells is responsible for formation of the ectopic muscle islands.
evidence: The manuscript presents images in Figure 8E showing ectopic islands in muscle-conditional heterozygous mice.

claim: A loss of Abl2 in myogenic cells is responsible for formation of the ectopic muscle islands.
source: Figure 8E shows that ectopic muscle islands form in Abl2f/+; Pax3cre mice, indicating that a loss of Abl2 in myogenic cells is responsible for formation of the ectopic muscle islands.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing ectopic islands form when Abl2 is conditionally inactivated in muscle precursors.

claim: Abl1−/− mice die at birth.
source: Although Abl2−/− mice survive postnatally, Abl1−/− mice die at birth (Tybulewicz et al., 1991).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on Abl1 mutant mice.

claim: Abl2−/− mice survive postnatally.
source: Although Abl2−/− mice survive postnatally, Abl1−/− mice die at birth (Tybulewicz et al., 1991).
evidence: The manuscript states this as a known fact about Abl2 mutant mice.

claim: Muscle fiber development appears normal in Abl1−/− mice.
source: Muscle fiber development appeared normal in Abl1−/− mice, as muscle fibers extend radially from the rib cage, converge medially around the central tendon, and attach to the central tendon (Hallock, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work showing normal muscle development in Abl1 mutants.

claim: Pre-positioned tendon cells are not essential to define the length and orientation of myofibers.
source: These findings indicate that pre-positioned tendon cells are not essential to define the length and orientation of myofibers.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that myofibers within ectopic islands are uniform in length and orientation despite not being in contact with pre-positioned specialized tendon cells.

claim: A pioneering myotube may induce tendon cells to organize and direct the orientation of later forming myotubes.
source: Because specialized tendon cells form at the ends of these muscle islands, our results raise the possibility that a pioneering myotube induces tendon cells to organize and direct the orientation of later forming myotubes.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on this possibility based on the observation that specialized tendon cells form at the ends of ectopic muscle islands.

claim: Increased myoblast proliferation during early embryonic development may favor longitudinal lengthening of muscle fibers rather than an increase in myofiber diameter.
source: It is possible that increased myoblast proliferation during early embryonic development favors longitudinal lengthening of muscle fibers rather than an increase in myofiber diameter.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on this possibility based on the observation that Abl2 mutants show increased length without increased diameter.

claim: In adult myofibers, increased satellite cell proliferation may lead to satellite cell fusion all along the myofiber, favoring an increase in muscle fiber diameter and muscle hypertrophy.
source: In contrast, in adult myofibers, increased satellite cell proliferation may lead to satellite cell fusion all along the myofiber, favoring an increase in muscle fiber diameter and muscle hypertrophy.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on this possibility to contrast with embryonic myogenesis.

claim: Abl2 attenuates myoblast proliferation, limiting expansion of the myoblast pool and muscle growth.
source: Here, we provide evidence that Abl2 attenuates myoblast proliferation, limiting expansion of the myoblast pool and muscle growth.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased myoblast proliferation in Abl2 mutants.

claim: Abl2 does not act primarily to regulate myoblast migration.
source: Although intercostal and diaphragm muscles develop through non-migratory and migratory mechanisms, respectively, Abl2 has a role in governing muscle length in both muscles, indicating that Abl2 does not act primarily, if at all to regulate myoblast migration.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that Abl2 affects muscle length in muscles that develop through different mechanisms.

claim: Migration of muscle precursors to the limb, but not the diaphragm, is perturbed in Lbx1 mutant mice.
source: There is precedence for differing requirements for the development of diaphragm and limb muscles: although both limb and diaphragm muscles are derived from Lbx1-expressing precursors, migration of muscle precursors to the limb, but not the diaphragm, is perturbed in Lbx1 mutant mice (Gross et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on Lbx1 mutant mice.

claim: The development of diaphragm and limb muscles differ in their requirement for Abl2.
source: Thus, the development of diaphragm and limb muscles differ in their requirement for Abl2, as well as Lbx1.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing Abl2 affects diaphragm but not limb muscles.

claim: In Drosophila, muscle cells provide signals to tendon cells to induce their differentiation.
source: In Drosophila, there is good evidence that muscle cells provide signals to tendon cells to induce their differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript cites this as established knowledge from Drosophila studies.

claim: Muscle cells in Drosophila produce Vein, a Neuregulin-like protein, which binds to the EGFR in adjacent tendon cells to mutually promote tendon cell differentiation.
source: Muscle cells produce Vein, a Neuregulin-like protein, which binds to the EGFR in adjacent tendon cells to mutually promote tendon cell differentiation (Yarnitzky et al., 1997; Volk, 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on muscle-tendon signaling in Drosophila.

claim: Activation of the EGFR in tendon cells enhances expression of Stripe and Slit, which signals back to Robo in muscle cells, contributing to muscle-specific tendon attachment.
source: Activation of the EGFR in tendon cells enhances expression of Stripe and Slit, which signals back to Robo in muscle cells, contributing to muscle-specific tendon attachment (Kramer et al., 2001; Volohonsky et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on muscle-tendon signaling in Drosophila.

claim: Muscle is required for tendon formation in the developing myotome and adjacent sclerotome.
source: Although there is evidence supporting the idea that muscle and tendon cells signal to one another in vertebrates, these studies have largely focused upon TGF- and FGF-dependent signaling between the developing myotome and the adjacent sclerotome, where muscle is required for tendon formation (Brent et al., 2003; Schweitzer et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on muscle-tendon signaling in vertebrates.

claim: The induction of head and limb tendons does not depend upon muscle.
